newsitem.title: USA: Bear market may feast on employee stock options.
newsitem.headline: Bear market may feast on employee stock options.

text.p: If the bear market growls, employees could see the value of their company stock options devoured.

A market plunge could upset employees who were given the options as an "extra" and who "actually have no choice but to hold them," said Richard Semler, of Los Angeles, national director of executive performance and pay for Sibson & Co., a leading human resources consulting firm.

"These broad-based all-employee programmes are untested in a bear market," Semler said. "The question is whether all the employees you've given stock options are going to understand why something that had value suddenly has no value."
Giving corporate executives stock options has been an established practice, Semler notes, and "one can expect they (executives) are more sophisticated in these things."

If an employee was given an option when the share price was $50 and the share price rises to $60, the option is worth $10. However, if the stock market has a major correction and the stock's price drops to $40, the option is worth nothing.
The company's stock would have to rebound to $51 before the employee's option was worth a dollar.

"Typically, the option is a 10-year option," Semler said, "and over time the option will come back into value if the company does well. The difficulty is getting your typical employee to understand that if the option loses its value it could sit there with no value for several years."
"That horde of gold for employees is likely to disappear or to get a lot smaller" (over the near term,) he said.
"As long as the company is performing reasonably well," Semler advised, employees should be patient because "historically, the stock price will recover as the market recovers."
Periods during which a company's stock is depressed, though, could present a major employee relations problem for employers.

Increasingly, Semler said, companies favour giving stock options to employees as incentives because they link them to shareholder value and the company "does not have to pay out real cash" as if, say, they granted bonuses to a work team.
From almost no companies five years ago, he said, "you might have about 5 percent today that have broad-based employee stock option plans."

Shareholders must vote to give up a portion of their holdings to reward workers in this way. Last year, the average potential stock dilution from new stock option plans increased 1 percentage point over 1995 to 4.9 percent, according to the Investor Responsibility Research Centre, of Washington, D.C.
In theory, motivating employees "to act more like owners," Semler said, will improve company performance, thus hiking the value of the shares remaining in shareholders' hands.

While broad-based employee stock option plans "can be a wonderful (employee) motivator if you're trying to get everybody to engage in a major turnaround," Semler said, their drawback for the long haul is that their value is pegged to the market price and beyond employees' control.
"The best motivators," Semler believes, "are those programmes that employees can see the impact of their achievements on and be rewarded for.

"There's some question whether stock options for all employees are an unadulterated good," Semler said. What is "good and healthy," he concluded, "is the corporation recognising that their primary reason for existence is to increase the wealth of its shareholders.
"This does not mean that shareholders will authorise unlimited shares to fund broad-based employee stock option plans even if, philosopically, they like them," Semler concluded.
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
